parsed_answer.content:
Over-engineering in enterprise software is a silent killer of maintainability, developer velocity, and runtime performance. Developers frequently introduce speculative generalization, designing for requirements that do not yet exist under the guise of future-proofing. In Core Java applications, this manifests as an obsession with abstraction layers: writing generic interfaces with single implementations, creating intricate factory hierarchies where a simple constructor would suffice, and overusing reflection or dynamic proxies where static dispatch provides superior performance and compiler safety. These patterns violate the YAGNI (You Aren't Gonna Need It) and KISS (Keep It Simple, Stupid) principles, introducing cognitive load and structural friction.

The manifestations of over-engineering are deeply rooted in resume-driven development and cargo-cult patterns borrowed from frameworks, improperly applied to foundational code. When every utility method is wrapped in a static factory, every domain object has a parallel DTO mapped via heavy reflection libraries, and every execution path uses functional composition where a straightforward for-loop is cleaner, the application suffers. In the JVM ecosystem, these unnecessary abstractions allocate excessive short-lived objects on the heap, increase GC pressure, pollute CPU instruction caches through virtual method dispatch and interface polymorphic call sites, and obscure the actual domain logic behind layers of boilerplate.

rows: AbstractFactory<T, V, R> with dynamic classpath scanning
Direct constructor invocation or standard factory method
Interfaces for every single class, regardless of implementation count
Concrete classes, refactoring to interfaces only when a second implementation arises
Three layers of mapping (Entity -> Domain -> DTO -> Response)
Exposing domain entities or direct record mapping where boundaries align
Custom checked exception hierarchies wrapping standard failures
Unchecked RuntimeExceptions with meaningful context messages

items: Speculative Generics: Adding type parameters like <T extends Serializable & Comparable<T>> to internal utility classes that only ever process Strings or Longs, destroying readability without adding type safety.

The Singleton Anti-Pattern: Implementing complex double-checked locking singletons or container-managed singletons for stateless utility classes instead of utilizing simple static methods or natural JVM classloading mechanics.
Over-Abstraction of Collections: Wrapping java.util.List inside custom wrapper classes that expose only a subset of methods, forcing boilerplate delegation and blocking efficient stream operations.
Premature Concurrency: Introducing CompletableFuture chains and ExecutorServices for synchronous tasks that execute sequentially, introducing context-switching overhead and debugging nightmares.

parsed_answer.content: Beware of the 'Enterprise Pattern' trap where design patterns from the 1994 Gang of Four book are applied indiscriminately to solve simple CRUD problems. Every layer of abstraction you add hides execution flow from the debugger, increases the bytecode size pushed through the JIT compiler's inline limits, and makes it harder for the next engineer to reason about system behavior during an outage.
